name: Brain
description: Cerebral cortex (gyri of both hemispheres), deep structures, ventricles, brainstem and cerebellum.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Brain
groups.tip: Your brain has three main parts: the big forebrain on top, a small midbrain, and the hindbrain at the back. This model leaves out a little of the cortex at the very front.

groups.label: Left cerebral hemisphere (gyri)
groups.tip: The central groove splits the jobs: the fold in front moves you, the fold behind feels. In most people the left half runs language, both speaking and understanding.

groups.label: Right cerebral hemisphere (gyri)
groups.tip: Each half of the brain moves and feels the opposite side of your body. The right half is great with spaces, faces and the feeling in a voice.

groups.label: Deep structures
groups.tip: The caudate and putamen team up as the striatum, a movement helper. The hippocampus stores memories, the amygdala sounds the fear alarm, and the fornix arches between them.

groups.label: Ventricles
groups.tip: Follow the fluid: from the two side ventricles into the third, down a narrow aqueduct to the fourth, then out to bathe the brain and spinal cord.

groups.label: Brainstem and cerebellum
groups.tip: Use the rule of fours: cranial nerves three and four leave the midbrain, five to eight the pons, and nine to twelve the medulla. Nerves one and two join the forebrain.

content.origin: From the Latin for forehead and the Greek gyros, a ring. A gyrus is one of the raised folds on the surface of the brain.
content.location: The topmost fold at the front of the left hemisphere, running front to back beside the midline. It rolls over onto the inner face of the hemisphere.
content.description: A long strip of cortex with a groove below it and the movement strip behind it. This model leaves out the very front tip and the lowest frontal fold.
content.function: Its back part, on the inner face, helps you plan and sequence movements. The rest helps with self-awareness, holding things in mind and controlling your behaviour.
content.mnemonic: Think of the frontal lobe as the front office. This fold is the top floor, where the plans are made.
content.clinical: Damage to the frontal lobes, including this fold, can change personality, drive and judgement. A stroke of the anterior cerebral artery hits its inner face.
content.hint: The top fold at the front of the hemisphere, running beside the deep groove that splits the brain in two.

questions.text: Which fold forms the top of the frontal lobe, next to the midline?
questions.explanation: The superior frontal gyrus runs along the top of the frontal lobe, next to the deep groove between the hemispheres.

content.origin: From the Latin for middle and forehead. It is the middle fold on the side of the frontal lobe.
content.location: On the outer side of the left frontal lobe, between two long grooves and just in front of the movement strip.
content.description: A broad fold running front to back, often split by a shallow groove. This model leaves out the lowest frontal fold beneath it.
content.function: Its back part, the frontal eye field, turns both eyes towards the opposite side when you choose to look. Its front part helps with planning, attention and holding information in mind.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the mind's eye. It steers your gaze and holds your plans in mind.
content.clinical: After a stroke that damages the frontal eye field, the eyes tend to drift towards the side of the damaged hemisphere.
content.hint: The fold across the middle of the side of the frontal lobe, between the top fold and the missing lowest one.

questions.text: Which area at the back of the middle frontal gyrus controls the eye movements you choose to make?
questions.explanation: The frontal eye field sits at the back of this fold. It turns your eyes when you decide where to look.

content.origin: From the Latin for in front of the centre. It is the fold just in front of the central groove.
content.location: The last fold of the left frontal lobe, just in front of the central groove. It runs from the top of the brain down towards the deep side groove.
content.description: A long, upright strip of cortex holding a map of the body. The leg is near the top, then the trunk, arm and hand, with the face lowest.
content.function: This is the main movement area, the primary motor cortex. It sends commands down to the muscles on the right side of your body.
content.mnemonic: Pre means go: the precentral strip makes you move, and the postcentral strip behind it lets you feel.
content.clinical: A stroke here weakens the right side of the body. Middle cerebral artery strokes mostly hit the face and arm, and anterior cerebral artery strokes the leg.
content.hint: The upright strip just in front of the central groove, holding the body map for movement.

questions.text: The precentral gyrus contains which area?
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. It sends the commands that move your muscles.

questions.text: A stroke in the left precentral gyrus would most likely cause what?
options: Weakness of the left side of the body
Loss of vision in both eyes
Weakness of the right side of the body
questions.explanation: Each side of the brain moves the opposite side of the body, because the movement pathway crosses over in the medulla.

content.origin: From the Latin for behind the centre. It is the fold just behind the central groove.
content.location: The first fold of the left parietal lobe, just behind the central groove and running alongside the movement strip.
content.description: A long, upright strip holding a map of body feeling. The hands and lips get huge areas, because they are so sensitive.
content.function: This is the main touch area. It receives touch, pain, temperature and body position from the right side of your body, passed up through the thalamus.
content.mnemonic: Post as in post office: this strip receives all the incoming mail from your skin.
content.clinical: Damage here dulls fine touch and position sense on the right side. It becomes hard to recognise objects just by feeling them.
content.hint: The upright strip just behind the central groove, the first stop in the cortex for touch.

questions.text: The postcentral gyrus lies in which lobe?
questions.explanation: It is the front fold of the parietal lobe, just behind the central groove.

questions.text: Which sensation is handled mainly in the postcentral gyrus?
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus is the main touch area. It also handles pain, temperature and body position.

content.origin: From the Latin paries, a wall, because the parietal bones form the side walls of the skull. Lobule means small lobe.
content.location: The upper back part of the left parietal lobe, behind the touch strip. It rolls over onto the inner face of the hemisphere.
content.description: A block of cortex high on the side of the parietal lobe. In this model it is joined with the precuneus, its partner on the inner face.
content.function: It blends touch, body position and vision into a sense of where your body and nearby objects are. This guides you when you reach out and grab something.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as your body's sat-nav. It always knows where your limbs are.
content.clinical: Damage can make it hard to reach accurately for things you can see. It can also blur the sense of where your right limbs are.
content.hint: The upper back part of the parietal lobe, above a deep groove, wrapping onto the inner face.

questions.text: What is the main role of the superior parietal lobule?
options: Blending touch and vision to sense where you are
questions.explanation: It combines touch and vision to track where your body is in space. This helps you reach and grab.

content.origin: From the Latin for above the edge. It arches over the end of the deep side groove.
content.location: In the lower part of the left parietal lobe, curving around the back end of the lateral sulcus, the deep groove on the side of the brain.
content.description: A horseshoe-shaped fold capping the end of the deep side groove. The angular gyrus lies just behind it.
content.function: It helps with touch, body position and planning skilled movements you have learned. On the left, the usual language side, it also helps you handle the sounds of words.
content.mnemonic: Supramarginal sits on the margin, capping the end of the side groove.
content.clinical: Damage here on the left can cause apraxia. Strength is normal, but the person struggles to make learned gestures, like waving goodbye, when asked.
content.hint: The horseshoe fold capping the back end of the deep side groove, just behind the lower touch strip.

questions.text: The supramarginal gyrus curves around the end of which groove?
questions.explanation: It caps the back end of the lateral sulcus, the deep groove on the side of the brain.

content.origin: From the Latin for angle or bend. It bends around the end of a groove in the temporal lobe.
content.location: At the back of the lower left parietal lobe, behind the supramarginal gyrus and close to the occipital lobe.
content.description: A curved fold sitting where three lobes meet: the parietal, temporal and occipital.
content.function: It links what you see, hear and feel. On the left, the usual language side, it is key for reading, writing, sums and the meaning of words.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the reading corner, the bend where seeing words meets understanding them.
content.clinical: Damage on the left can cause Gerstmann syndrome. The person struggles to write and do sums, mixes up left and right, and cannot name their fingers.
content.hint: The curved fold where three lobes meet, just behind the horseshoe that caps the deep side groove.

questions.text: Damage to the left angular gyrus is most likely to affect which ability?
questions.explanation: On the left, the angular gyrus is key for reading, writing and doing sums.

content.origin: From the Latin tempus, meaning time. It names the temples, where hair often turns grey first with age.
content.location: The top fold of the left temporal lobe, just below the deep side groove. Its hidden upper surface carries small folds that receive sound.
content.description: A long fold running front to back. In this model it includes Heschl's gyri, the small folds on its top surface where hearing arrives.
content.function: Its top surface is the main hearing area, getting sound from both ears. At the back on the left, the Wernicke area helps you understand what people say.
content.mnemonic: Superior temporal means superior hearing. Your ears sit right beside your temporal lobes.
content.clinical: Damage to the Wernicke area causes Wernicke aphasia. Speech flows easily but makes little sense, and the person struggles to understand others.
content.hint: The top fold of the lobe beside the ear, just below the deep side groove, with a hidden surface that receives sound.

questions.text: The small folds on top of the superior temporal gyrus hold which area?
questions.explanation: Heschl's gyri hold the primary auditory cortex. This is where hearing first reaches the cortex.

questions.text: Damage to the back of the left superior temporal gyrus usually causes which problem?
questions.explanation: This is the Wernicke area. Damage causes Wernicke aphasia, where understanding speech becomes hard.

content.origin: From the Latin for middle and temple. It is the middle fold on the side of the temporal lobe.
content.location: On the outer side of the left temporal lobe, between the top and bottom temporal folds.
content.description: A long fold running front to back between two grooves, stretching back towards the occipital lobe.
content.function: It links words and sights to their meaning and holds memory for facts. Its back end spots movement, and on the left it is part of the language network.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the middle man, linking sounds and sights to what they mean.
content.clinical: Epilepsy and tumours often involve this fold. Damage on the left can make it hard to find the right word.
content.hint: The middle of three long folds on the side of the lobe beside the ear.

questions.text: Which fold lies between the superior and inferior temporal gyri?
questions.explanation: The middle temporal gyrus sits between them, just as its name suggests.

content.origin: From the Latin for lower and temple. It is the lowest fold on the side of the temporal lobe.
content.location: The lowest fold on the side of the left temporal lobe, curling under onto the base of the brain.
content.description: A long fold forming the lower outer edge of the temporal lobe, with the fusiform gyrus beside it underneath.
content.function: It is part of the what pathway of vision. It helps you recognise objects, shapes and colours.
content.mnemonic: Inferior temporal for identifying things. It answers the question, what am I looking at?
content.clinical: Damage along this pathway can cause visual agnosia. The person sees an object clearly but cannot tell what it is.
content.hint: The lowest fold on the side of the lobe beside the ear, curling under onto the base of the brain.

questions.text: The inferior temporal gyrus is part of which vision pathway?
options: The what pathway, for recognising objects
The where pathway, for locating things
The reflex pathway to the midbrain
questions.explanation: It sits on the what pathway. This stream of vision works out what an object is.

content.origin: From the Latin occiput, the back of the head.
content.location: The back lobe of the left hemisphere, behind the parietal and temporal lobes. It rests on a sheet of tough tissue above the cerebellum.
content.description: A pyramid-shaped lobe. On its inner face, a deep groove called the calcarine sulcus splits it into an upper and a lower part.
content.function: This is your seeing lobe. The main vision area lines the calcarine sulcus and receives the right half of what both eyes see.
content.mnemonic: O for optic: the occipital lobe does your seeing, at the back of your head.
content.clinical: A stroke in one occipital lobe blanks out the opposite half of vision in both eyes. The very centre of vision is often spared.
content.hint: The back lobe of the hemisphere, sitting above the cerebellum, with a deep groove on its inner face.

questions.text: The main vision area lines which groove in the occipital lobe?
questions.explanation: The primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus, on the inner face of the occipital lobe.

questions.text: A stroke in the left occipital lobe would blank out which part of vision?
options: The right half of vision in both eyes
The left half of vision in both eyes
All vision in the left eye only
questions.explanation: Each occipital lobe sees the opposite half of the world. So damage on the left blanks the right half in both eyes.

content.origin: From the Latin for island. It is an island of cortex hidden deep inside the side groove.
content.location: Deep inside the left lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. You only see it when you pull the lips of the groove apart.
content.description: A triangle of cortex with short and long folds, ringed by a groove, like a buried island.
content.function: It is your main taste area. It also senses what is going on inside you, like heartbeat, breathing and gut feelings, and links them to emotion.
content.mnemonic: Insula sounds like inside. It is the hidden island that feels your insides.
content.clinical: Middle cerebral artery strokes often damage the insula, because the artery's branches run right over it.
content.hint: Cortex hidden deep in the side groove, covered by the lips of three lobes, where taste is handled.

questions.text: Where is the insula found?
options: On the inner face of the occipital lobe
On the top of the frontal lobe
questions.explanation: The insula is hidden deep inside the lateral sulcus, covered by the lips of three lobes.

questions.text: Which main sense area is found in the insula?
questions.explanation: The insula holds the main taste area, the gustatory cortex.

content.origin: From the Latin for belt. It wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.
content.location: On the inner face of the left hemisphere, arching over the corpus callosum from front to back.
content.description: A C-shaped fold sitting between two grooves. Behind the corpus callosum it narrows and flows into the parahippocampal gyrus.
content.function: It is part of the limbic system, your emotional brain. The front helps with emotion, motivation, attention and how bad pain feels, and the back helps with memory.
content.mnemonic: Cingulate sounds like cingulum, a belt. It belts around the corpus callosum.
content.clinical: Swelling in one hemisphere can push this fold under the tough midline sheet, the falx. This is called subfalcine herniation and can squeeze the anterior cerebral arteries.
content.hint: A belt of cortex on the inner face, curving right over the big white bridge between the hemispheres.

questions.text: The cingulate gyrus arches just above which structure?
questions.explanation: It wraps over the top of the corpus callosum, the bridge between the two hemispheres.

questions.text: The name cingulate comes from the Latin for what?
questions.explanation: Cingulum means belt. This fold belts around the corpus callosum.

content.origin: From the Greek for beside the seahorse. It is the fold next to the hippocampus.
content.location: On the underside and inner face of the left temporal lobe, next to the hippocampus, with the fusiform gyrus on its outer side.
content.description: A fold whose front end hooks back on itself, forming the uncus. Its front part is the main gateway into the hippocampus.
content.function: It passes information from the cortex into the hippocampus to make new memories. It also helps you recognise places and scenes.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the hippocampus's partner, feeding new memories in.
content.clinical: Raised pressure can push its hook, the uncus, over a tough edge. This squeezes the nerve that works the eye and makes the pupil on that side go wide.
content.hint: The inner fold under the lobe beside the ear, lying next to the seahorse-shaped memory maker and ending in a hook.

questions.text: The parahippocampal gyrus feeds information into which structure to make memories?
questions.explanation: Its front part is the main way into the hippocampus, where new memories are formed.

content.origin: From the Latin for spindle-shaped. It is wide in the middle and tapers at each end.
content.location: On the underside of the left temporal and occipital lobes, between the inferior temporal gyrus and the parahippocampal gyrus.
content.description: A long, spindle-shaped fold on the base of the brain, separated from its inner neighbour by a groove.
content.function: It is a high-level vision area for recognising faces. On the left it also holds a word area that you use when you read.
content.mnemonic: Fusiform for faces: both start with F.
content.clinical: Damage to the face area, especially on the right or both sides, can cause face blindness. The person can no longer recognise familiar faces.
content.hint: A spindle-shaped fold on the base of the brain, between the lowest side fold and the fold next to the memory maker.

questions.text: Damage to the fusiform gyrus may cause which condition?
questions.explanation: The fusiform gyrus holds a special face area. Damage can make familiar faces impossible to recognise.

content.clinical: Damage can make it hard to reach accurately for things you can see. It can also blur the sense of where your left limbs are.

content.origin: From the Latin for above the edge. It arches over the end of the deep side groove.
content.location: In the lower part of the right parietal lobe, curving around the back end of the lateral sulcus, the deep groove on the side of the brain.

content.function: It helps with touch, body position and planning skilled movements you have learned. On the right, it helps with spatial attention and sensing how others feel.
content.mnemonic: Supramarginal sits on the margin, capping the end of the side groove.
content.clinical: Apraxia, trouble making learned gestures when asked despite normal strength, mainly follows damage to this area on the left side.
content.hint: The horseshoe fold capping the back end of the deep side groove, just behind the lower touch strip.

content.origin: From the Latin for angle or bend. It bends around the end of a groove in the temporal lobe.
content.location: At the back of the lower right parietal lobe, behind the supramarginal gyrus and close to the occipital lobe.
content.description: A curved fold sitting where three lobes meet: the parietal, temporal and occipital.
content.function: It links what you see, hear and feel. On the right, it helps with spatial attention, and damage in this region can make a person ignore the left side of space.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the reading corner, the bend where seeing words meets understanding them.
content.clinical: Gerstmann syndrome, with trouble writing, doing sums, telling left from right and naming fingers, follows damage to this area on the left side.
content.hint: The curved fold where three lobes meet, just behind the horseshoe that caps the deep side groove.

content.location: The top fold of the right temporal lobe, just below the deep side groove. Its hidden upper surface carries small folds that receive sound.

content.mnemonic: Superior temporal means superior hearing. Your ears sit right beside your temporal lobes.
content.clinical: Wernicke aphasia, where speech flows but makes little sense, usually follows damage on the left. Damage here on the right can make it hard to read the tone of a voice.
content.hint: The top fold of the lobe beside the ear, just below the deep side groove, with a hidden surface that receives sound.

content.origin: From the Latin for middle and temple. It is the middle fold on the side of the temporal lobe.
content.location: On the outer side of the right temporal lobe, between the top and bottom temporal folds.
content.description: A long fold running front to back between two grooves, stretching back towards the occipital lobe.
content.function: It links words and sights to their meaning and holds memory for facts. Its back end, near the occipital lobe, helps you spot movement.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the middle man, linking sounds and sights to what they mean.
content.clinical: Epilepsy and tumours often involve this fold. Word-finding trouble is more likely when the left one is damaged.
content.hint: The middle of three long folds on the side of the lobe beside the ear.

content.origin: From the Latin for lower and temple. It is the lowest fold on the side of the temporal lobe.
content.location: The lowest fold on the side of the right temporal lobe, curling under onto the base of the brain.
content.description: A long fold forming the lower outer edge of the temporal lobe, with the fusiform gyrus beside it underneath.

content.hint: The lowest fold on the side of the lobe beside the ear, curling under onto the base of the brain.

content.origin: From the Latin occiput, the back of the head.
content.location: The back lobe of the right hemisphere, behind the parietal and temporal lobes. It rests on a sheet of tough tissue above the cerebellum.
content.description: A pyramid-shaped lobe. On its inner face, a deep groove called the calcarine sulcus splits it into an upper and a lower part.
content.function: This is your seeing lobe. The main vision area lines the calcarine sulcus and receives the left half of what both eyes see.
content.mnemonic: O for optic: the occipital lobe does your seeing, at the back of your head.
content.clinical: A stroke in one occipital lobe blanks out the opposite half of vision in both eyes. The very centre of vision is often spared.
content.hint: The back lobe of the hemisphere, sitting above the cerebellum, with a deep groove on its inner face.

content.origin: From the Latin for island. It is an island of cortex hidden deep inside the side groove.
content.location: Deep inside the right lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. You only see it when you pull the lips of the groove apart.

content.function: It is your main taste area. It also senses what is going on inside you, like heartbeat, breathing and gut feelings, and links them to emotion.
content.mnemonic: Insula sounds like inside. It is the hidden island that feels your insides.
content.clinical: Middle cerebral artery strokes often damage the insula, because the artery's branches run right over it.
content.hint: Cortex hidden deep in the side groove, covered by the lips of three lobes, where taste is handled.

content.origin: From the Latin for belt. It wraps around the corpus callosum like a belt.
content.location: On the inner face of the right hemisphere, arching over the corpus callosum from front to back.
content.description: A C-shaped fold sitting between two grooves. Behind the corpus callosum it narrows and flows into the parahippocampal gyrus.
content.function: It is part of the limbic system, your emotional brain. The front helps with emotion, motivation, attention and how bad pain feels, and the back helps with memory.

content.hint: A belt of cortex on the inner face, curving right over the big white bridge between the hemispheres.

content.origin: From the Latin for spindle-shaped. It is wide in the middle and tapers at each end.

content.description: A long, spindle-shaped fold on the base of the brain, separated from its inner neighbour by a groove.
content.function: It is a high-level vision area for recognising faces. The right side usually does more of the face work than the left.
content.mnemonic: Fusiform for faces: both start with F.
content.clinical: Damage to the face area, especially on the right or both sides, can cause face blindness. The person can no longer recognise familiar faces.
content.hint: A spindle-shaped fold on the base of the brain, between the lowest side fold and the fold next to the memory maker.

content.origin: From the Latin for tough body.
content.location: Deep in the middle, at the bottom of the groove that splits the brain in two. It joins the two hemispheres and forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
content.description: A thick, curved band of white matter, the biggest bridge in the brain. From front to back its parts are the rostrum, genu, body and splenium.
content.function: It carries hundreds of millions of nerve fibres between the left and right hemispheres. This lets the two halves share information and work as a team.
content.mnemonic: Callosum connects. It is the bridge between your two brain halves.
content.clinical: Surgeons sometimes cut it to stop severe seizures spreading from one side to the other. Afterwards the two halves struggle to share information, called split brain.
content.hint: The big arched white bridge in the midline between the two hemispheres, with a belt of cortex curving above it.

questions.text: What is the main job of the corpus callosum?
options: Connecting the left and right hemispheres
questions.explanation: It is the biggest bridge in the brain, carrying fibres between the left and right hemispheres.

questions.text: Which part of the corpus callosum is at its back end?
questions.explanation: The splenium is the thick back end of the corpus callosum.

content.origin: From the Greek for inner chamber or bedroom.
content.location: Deep in the centre of the brain on the left side, above the hypothalamus. It forms the side wall of the third ventricle.
content.description: An egg-shaped lump of grey matter made of many nuclei. The two thalami are often joined across the middle by a small bridge.
content.function: It is the main relay to the cortex. Almost every sense except smell passes through it, and it also helps keep you alert and awake.
content.mnemonic: Think of the thalamus as the brain's switchboard. Every sense except smell is switched through it.
content.clinical: A stroke here can cause numbness on the right side of the body. Sometimes a severe burning pain follows later.
content.hint: An egg-shaped grey lump in the centre of the brain, forming the side wall of the slit-like middle cavity.

questions.text: Which sense does NOT pass through the thalamus on its way to the cortex?
questions.explanation: Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without stopping at the thalamus.

questions.text: The thalamus forms the side wall of which ventricle?
questions.explanation: The two thalami face each other across the third ventricle, forming its side walls.

content.origin: From the Greek for inner chamber or bedroom.
content.location: Deep in the centre of the brain on the right side, above the hypothalamus. It forms the side wall of the third ventricle.
content.description: An egg-shaped lump of grey matter made of many nuclei. The two thalami are often joined across the middle by a small bridge.
content.function: It is the main relay to the cortex. Almost every sense except smell passes through it, and it also helps keep you alert and awake.
content.mnemonic: Think of the thalamus as the brain's switchboard. Every sense except smell is switched through it.
content.clinical: A stroke here can cause numbness on the left side of the body. Sometimes a severe burning pain follows later.
content.hint: An egg-shaped grey lump in the centre of the brain, forming the side wall of the slit-like middle cavity.

content.origin: From the Greek for below the inner chamber. It is the part below the thalamus.
content.location: Just below the thalamus, in the floor of the third ventricle. It sits above the pituitary gland and behind the optic chiasm.
content.description: A small cluster of nuclei about the size of an almond. The pituitary hangs from its underside on a stalk.
content.function: It keeps your body in balance, running temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep. It also controls the pituitary and makes the hormones ADH and oxytocin.
content.mnemonic: The hypothalamus runs the four Fs: feeding, fighting, fleeing and reproduction.
content.clinical: Damage here or to the pituitary stalk can stop ADH release. This causes diabetes insipidus, with huge amounts of watery urine and constant thirst.
content.hint: A small region below the central relay, in the floor of the middle cavity, with the hormone gland hanging from it on a stalk.

questions.text: Which of these is a main job of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus keeps your body in balance, including temperature, hunger and thirst.

questions.text: The hypothalamus controls which gland through a stalk?
questions.explanation: The pituitary hangs from the hypothalamus on a stalk and takes its orders from it.

content.origin: From the Latin for phlegm, because people once thought it made nasal mucus. Its other name, hypophysis, means undergrowth in Greek.
content.location: At the base of the brain in the middle, in a saddle-shaped hollow of the sphenoid bone. It hangs from the hypothalamus, just below the optic chiasm.
content.description: A gland about the size of a pea, with a front lobe and a back lobe.
content.function: The front lobe makes hormones that control growth and other glands, like the thyroid. The back lobe releases ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the hypothalamus.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the master gland with a boss. It controls other glands but takes orders from the hypothalamus.
content.clinical: A pituitary tumour growing upwards can press on the optic chiasm. This blanks out the outer half of vision in both eyes.
content.hint: The pea-sized gland in a bony saddle at the base of the skull, hanging on a stalk just below where the eye nerves cross.

questions.text: A pituitary tumour pressing upwards usually causes which vision problem?
options: Double vision only when looking down
Loss of the lower half of vision
Loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes
questions.explanation: It squeezes the crossing fibres in the optic chiasm. These carry the outer half of vision from each eye.

questions.text: The pituitary gland sits in a hollow of which bone?
questions.explanation: It sits in the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped hollow in the sphenoid bone.

content.origin: From the Latin for pine cone, because of its shape.
content.location: In the middle at the back of the third ventricle, just above the top of the midbrain and below the back end of the corpus callosum.
content.description: A tiny gland shaped like a pine cone. In adults it often contains small specks of calcium.
content.function: It makes the hormone melatonin, mostly at night in the dark. This helps set your daily sleep and wake rhythm, your body clock.
content.mnemonic: Pine cone at night: the pineal makes melatonin when the lights go out.
content.clinical: With age it often gathers calcium and shows up on scans as a handy midline marker. A pineal tumour can block the aqueduct and cause fluid build-up in the brain.
content.hint: A tiny cone-shaped gland at the back of the middle cavity, perched above the top of the brainstem.

questions.text: Which hormone does the pineal gland make?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland makes melatonin, which helps control your sleep and wake cycle.

content.origin: From the Greek for horse and sea monster. Its curled shape looks like a seahorse.
content.location: Deep in the inner part of the left temporal lobe, forming the floor of the lower horn of the lateral ventricle. It lies just behind the amygdala.
content.description: A curved ridge of grey matter shaped like a seahorse. Only the left one is shown here, and a matching one sits on the right.
content.function: It is essential for making new memories of facts and events. It also helps you remember places and find your way around.
content.mnemonic: The hippo goes to campus to learn. The hippocampus is your memory maker.
content.clinical: Alzheimer disease damages the hippocampus early, which is why recent memories fade first. It is also a common source of temporal lobe epilepsy.
content.hint: A seahorse-shaped ridge deep in the inner temporal lobe, forming the floor of a horn of the fluid cavity.

questions.text: What is the main job of the hippocampus?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is essential for making new memories of facts and events.

questions.text: Which disease usually damages the hippocampus early, causing loss of recent memories?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer disease strikes the hippocampus early, so making new memories becomes hard.

content.origin: From the Greek word for almond, because of its shape.
content.location: Deep in the front of the inner left temporal lobe, under the uncus. It sits just in front of the hippocampus.
content.description: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei. Only the left one is shown here, and a matching one sits on the right.
content.function: It spots danger and sets off fear and other strong emotions. It also makes memories of emotional events stronger.
content.mnemonic: Amygdala sounds like alarm. It is the almond-shaped alarm bell of your brain.
content.clinical: Damage to both amygdalae dampens normal fear. People also struggle to spot fear in other people's faces.
content.hint: An almond-shaped cluster at the front of the inner temporal lobe, just in front of the seahorse-shaped memory maker.

questions.text: Which emotion is most closely linked with the amygdala?
questions.explanation: The amygdala spots threats and sets off fear.

questions.text: The amygdala sits just in front of which structure?
questions.explanation: The amygdala lies at the front of the inner temporal lobe, just in front of the hippocampus.

content.origin: From the Latin cauda, meaning tail. This nucleus has a long tail.
content.location: Deep in the left hemisphere, hugging the wall of the lateral ventricle. Its big head bulges into the front horn.
content.description: A C-shaped nucleus with a large head, a body and a thin tail, one of the basal ganglia. Only the left one is shown, and a matching one sits on the right.
content.function: With the putamen it forms the striatum, the input to the basal ganglia. It helps start and control movement and plays a part in learning, habits and motivation.
content.mnemonic: The caudate has a tail. Add the putamen and you get the striped striatum.
content.clinical: In Huntington disease the caudate shrinks, so the front horns of the ventricles look bigger on scans. This causes jerky, uncontrolled movements called chorea.
content.hint: A C-shaped grey nucleus with a head and a tail, hugging the wall of the fluid cavity inside the hemisphere.

questions.text: Shrinking of the caudate nucleus is typical of which disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease makes the caudate shrink, leading to jerky movements.

questions.text: The caudate nucleus and putamen together form what?
questions.explanation: Together the caudate and putamen are called the striatum, which means striped.

content.origin: From the Latin for the shell or husk of a nut. It forms the outer shell of a lens-shaped nucleus.
content.location: Deep in the left hemisphere, outside the globus pallidus and just beneath the insula.
content.description: A rounded, shell-like mass forming the outer part of the lens-shaped lentiform nucleus. Only the left one is shown, and a matching one sits on the right.
content.function: It is part of the striatum, with the caudate. It takes in signals from the movement cortex and dopamine from the midbrain, and helps keep movement smooth.
content.mnemonic: Putamen is the outer shell, wrapped around the pale ball of the globus pallidus.
content.clinical: In Parkinson disease the putamen loses its dopamine supply first. It is also a common spot for bleeding in the brain caused by high blood pressure.
content.hint: The curved outer shell of the deep lens-shaped nucleus, tucked just under the hidden island of cortex.

questions.text: The putamen lies on which side of the globus pallidus?
questions.explanation: The putamen lies on the outer, lateral side of the globus pallidus. Together they make the lentiform nucleus.

content.origin: From the Latin for pale ball. It looks paler than the putamen because it is packed with insulated nerve fibres.
content.location: Deep in the left hemisphere, just inside the putamen and outside the internal capsule.
content.description: A pale, wedge-shaped mass in two parts, which forms the lentiform nucleus with the putamen. Only the left one is shown, and a matching one sits on the right.
content.function: It is the main exit of the basal ganglia. It sends braking signals to the thalamus, helping you pick the movements you want and block the ones you do not.
content.mnemonic: A pale ball in the middle: the globus pallidus sits inside the putamen's shell.
content.clinical: Deep brain stimulation of its inner part can ease movement disorders such as Parkinson disease and dystonia.
content.hint: The pale, wedge-shaped inner part of the lens-shaped deep nucleus, inside its outer shell.

questions.text: What is the main role of the globus pallidus?
options: Main exit of the basal ganglia to the thalamus
questions.explanation: Its inner part sends the main braking output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus.

content.origin: From the Latin for arch or vault.
content.location: It arches under the corpus callosum from the left hippocampus, forward over the third ventricle, then down to the mammillary body of the hypothalamus.
content.description: A C-shaped bundle of white-matter fibres. The two sides meet under the corpus callosum and part again at the front. Only the left one is shown.
content.function: It is the main exit cable of the hippocampus. It carries memory signals to the mammillary bodies and other parts of the limbic system.
content.mnemonic: Fornix, the forward arch: it arches forward from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
content.clinical: Damage to the fornix, for example during surgery on a cyst in the third ventricle, can make it hard to form new memories.
content.hint: An arched white cable curving under the midline bridge, running from the seahorse-shaped memory maker towards the hypothalamus.

questions.text: The fornix carries fibres out of which structure?
questions.explanation: The fornix is the main output cable of the hippocampus.

content.origin: From the Greek for a crossing, named after the X-shaped Greek letter chi.
content.location: At the base of the brain in the middle, above the pituitary gland and in front of its stalk, just below the front of the hypothalamus.
content.description: An X-shaped crossing where the two optic nerves meet, swap some fibres, then split into the two optic tracts.
content.function: Fibres from the inner, nose side of each retina cross over here. So each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the world from both eyes.
content.mnemonic: X marks the crossing. Only the nose-side fibres cross.
content.clinical: Pressure from below, usually a pituitary tumour, damages the crossing fibres. This blanks out the outer half of vision in both eyes.
content.hint: An X-shaped crossing at the base of the brain, just above the pea-sized gland, where the nerves from the eyes meet.

questions.text: Which fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
options: Fibres from the outer half of each retina
Fibres from the inner, nose-side half of each retina
questions.explanation: Only fibres from the nose side of each retina cross. They carry the outer half of each eye's view.

content.origin: From the Latin for little belly, and lateral, meaning at the side.
content.location: Inside the left hemisphere, under the corpus callosum. It curves from the frontal lobe back and then down into the temporal lobe.
content.description: A C-shaped cavity with horns reaching into the frontal, occipital and temporal lobes. Inside it, a spongy tissue called choroid plexus makes brain fluid.
content.function: It holds and makes cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain and carries away waste. The fluid flows out through a small hole into the third ventricle.
content.mnemonic: Follow the fluid: lateral to third, down the aqueduct to the fourth, then out around the brain.
content.clinical: If the fluid is blocked, the ventricles swell, called hydrocephalus, and pressure builds in the skull. A shunt tube can drain the extra fluid.
content.hint: The largest C-shaped fluid-filled cavity inside the hemisphere, with horns reaching into three lobes.

questions.text: Brain fluid flows from each lateral ventricle into which space?
questions.explanation: The fluid passes through a small hole on each side, the interventricular foramen, into the third ventricle.

questions.text: Which tissue in the ventricles makes cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus, a spongy tissue inside the ventricles, makes the fluid.

content.origin: From the Latin for little belly, and lateral, meaning at the side.
content.location: Inside the right hemisphere, under the corpus callosum. It curves from the frontal lobe back and then down into the temporal lobe.
content.description: A C-shaped cavity with horns reaching into the frontal, occipital and temporal lobes. Inside it, a spongy tissue called choroid plexus makes brain fluid.
content.function: It holds and makes cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain and carries away waste. The fluid flows out through a small hole into the third ventricle.
content.mnemonic: Follow the fluid: lateral to third, down the aqueduct to the fourth, then out around the brain.
content.clinical: If the fluid is blocked, the ventricles swell, called hydrocephalus, and pressure builds in the skull. A shunt tube can drain the extra fluid.
content.hint: The largest C-shaped fluid-filled cavity inside the hemisphere, with horns reaching into three lobes.

content.origin: From the Latin for third little belly.
content.location: In the middle of the brain, between the left and right thalami, with the hypothalamus in its floor.
content.description: A narrow, slit-like cavity. Small holes link it to each lateral ventricle, and the aqueduct links it to the fourth ventricle.
content.function: It passes brain fluid from the lateral ventricles on to the aqueduct. Choroid plexus in its roof adds more fluid.
content.mnemonic: The third is the thin one, a slit squeezed between the two thalami.
content.clinical: A small colloid cyst at its front can block the holes to the lateral ventricles. This causes sudden fluid build-up and headache.
content.hint: A thin slit of fluid in the midline, with an egg-shaped relay mass on each side.

questions.text: The third ventricle lies between which pair of structures?
questions.explanation: The third ventricle is a thin slit in the middle, between the two thalami.

content.origin: From the Latin for water and to lead. It is a channel that leads fluid along.
content.location: In the middle of the brain, running down through the midbrain from the third ventricle to the fourth.
content.description: A narrow canal about 1.5 centimetres long, the tightest point of the fluid system. Unlike the ventricles, it has no choroid plexus.
content.function: It carries brain fluid from the third ventricle down to the fourth ventricle.
content.mnemonic: Think of an aqueduct as a water pipe, running through the midbrain.
content.clinical: A narrowed aqueduct is a common cause of fluid build-up in the brain present at birth, because fluid cannot drain out of the third ventricle.
content.hint: The narrow fluid channel through the upper brainstem, linking the slit-like middle cavity to the tent-shaped one behind the pons.

questions.text: The cerebral aqueduct links which two ventricles?
questions.explanation: It runs through the midbrain from the third ventricle to the fourth.

content.origin: From the Latin for fourth little belly.
content.location: In the middle of the hindbrain, with the pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind.
content.description: A tent-shaped cavity with a diamond-shaped floor. Three openings let fluid out, and below it continues as the thin canal of the spinal cord.
content.function: It collects fluid from the aqueduct and adds more of its own. Then it lets the fluid out through three openings to bathe the brain and spinal cord.
content.mnemonic: Magendie in the middle, Luschka on the sides: the three exits of the fourth ventricle.
content.clinical: In children, tumours of the cerebellum or brainstem can block it. This causes fluid build-up with headache, vomiting and unsteadiness.
content.hint: A tent-shaped fluid cavity behind the pons and medulla, with the cerebellum as its roof.

questions.text: The fourth ventricle lies between the brainstem and which structure?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle has the brainstem in front and the cerebellum behind.

questions.text: How does brain fluid leave the ventricles?
options: Through the small holes between the ventricles
Through the three openings of the fourth ventricle
questions.explanation: Fluid escapes through the three openings of the fourth ventricle into the space around the brain.

content.origin: Its other name, mesencephalon, comes from the Greek for middle brain.
content.location: The top part of the brainstem, below the thalamus and hypothalamus and above the pons.
content.description: A short section with four small bumps on its back and the aqueduct through its middle. It holds a dark band of cells, the substantia nigra.
content.function: It carries messages between the brain above and the brainstem below. Its bumps handle quick seeing and hearing reflexes, and it is home to cranial nerves three and four.
content.mnemonic: The midbrain has three and four: the oculomotor and trochlear nerves start here.
content.clinical: In Parkinson disease, the dopamine-making cells of the substantia nigra die. This causes tremor, stiffness and slow movement.
content.hint: The top section of the brainstem, with four small bumps on its back and a narrow fluid channel through its centre.

questions.text: Parkinson disease involves loss of nerve cells in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation: The dopamine-making cells of the substantia nigra, in the midbrain, are lost in Parkinson disease.

questions.text: Which cranial nerves start in the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve, number three, and the trochlear nerve, number four, both start in the midbrain.

content.origin: From the Latin for bridge. It looks like a bridge between the two halves of the cerebellum.
content.location: The middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain above and the medulla below, with the cerebellum behind it.
content.description: A rounded bulge on the front of the brainstem, made of fibres running side to side. Thick stalks join it to the cerebellum on each side.
content.function: It relays messages from the cortex to the cerebellum and helps set your breathing rhythm. It is also home to cranial nerves five to eight, serving the face, eye and ear.
content.mnemonic: Pons means bridge. It bridges the cortex to the cerebellum.
content.clinical: A stroke in the front of the pons can cause locked-in syndrome. The person is fully awake but can only move their eyes up and down.
content.hint: The rounded bulge in the middle of the brainstem, between the top section and the lowest part that joins the spinal cord.

questions.text: Which part of the brainstem lies between the midbrain and the medulla?
questions.explanation: The pons is the middle part of the brainstem.

questions.text: Locked-in syndrome most often comes from damage to which structure?
questions.explanation: A stroke in the front of the pons cuts the movement pathways but leaves the person awake and aware.

content.origin: From the Latin medulla, meaning marrow or core, and oblongata, meaning stretched out.
content.location: The lowest part of the brainstem, below the pons and in front of the cerebellum. It becomes the spinal cord at the big hole in the base of the skull.
content.description: A cone-shaped section with two ridges called pyramids on its front. Here the movement fibres in the pyramids cross to the other side.
content.function: It runs your vital controls: heart rate, blood pressure and breathing. It also handles swallowing, coughing and being sick, and holds cranial nerves nine to twelve.
content.mnemonic: Medulla, most vital. Damage here can stop the control of breathing and heartbeat.
content.clinical: High pressure in the skull can force the bottom of the cerebellum down through the skull's big hole. This squeezes the medulla and can stop breathing.
content.hint: The bottom of the brainstem, narrowing into the spinal cord where it drops through the big hole in the skull.

questions.text: Which vital job is controlled by the medulla oblongata?
questions.explanation: The medulla holds the control centres for breathing and heart rate.

questions.text: Where do the main movement fibres cross to the other side?
questions.explanation: The movement fibres cross in the lower medulla, at the pyramids. That is why each side of the brain moves the opposite side.

content.origin: From the Latin for little brain.
content.location: At the back of your skull, tucked under the occipital lobes and behind the pons and medulla. A tough sheet of tissue separates it from the lobes above.
content.description: Two halves joined by a narrow middle strip, the vermis, covered in fine parallel folds. Inside, its white matter branches like a tree.
content.function: It fine-tunes movement, balance and posture, and helps you learn skills like riding a bike. Each side controls the same side of the body.
content.mnemonic: Think of it as the balance-ellum, the little brain that keeps you steady.
content.clinical: Damage, including from alcohol, makes a person unsteady and clumsy, with slurred speech. The problems show on the same side as the damage.
content.hint: The little brain with fine parallel folds, tucked under the back of the hemispheres, behind the brainstem.

questions.text: What is the main job of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture.

questions.text: Damage to the right side of the cerebellum causes poor coordination on which side?
questions.explanation: Each side of the cerebellum controls the same side of the body. So damage on the right affects the right.
